cover.alt: Night in a turf farmhouse in summer: a red-faced girl lies ill in bed with a wet cloth on her forehead; a young man sits on a bench beside the bed, reading aloud from a handwritten book on his knees.
cover.art_brief: Farm scene, ink and watercolour, no lettering anywhere (the book's pages show only grey lines). A cold, grey summer night, July 1882, the baðstofa at Hamrar: low turf-and-timber room, an open-bowl oil lamp (no glass chimney) on a shelf, a small window with grey light. Ásta (14, fair hair loose, no cap) lies ill in her bed under a woollen blanket, her face and hands red with the measles rash, a folded wet cloth (dúkur) on her forehead (enni), eyes half open, a faint smile. Siggi (19, fair, thin, woollen jacket) sits on a wooden bench beside the bed with afi's handwritten Edda open on his knees (kné), reading aloud. On a chest by the bed stands a small glass of water. Guðrún (about fifty, headscarf, a bunch of iron keys at her waist) stands at the foot of the bed. Gamla-Manga (very old, headscarf) sits on the next bed, listening. Snati the old sheepdog lies by the door. Quiet, tender, cool light; no religious images on the walls.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Kviða er kvæði sem segir sögu. Í bók afa eru margar kviður. Þrymskviða segir frá hamri Þórs, og frá brúðinni sem át einn uxa.
Afi sagði Þrymskviðu í óbundnu máli, og Ásta kunni hana utanbókar. Siggi les hana eins og skáldið orti hana, með stuðlum og höfuðstöfum.
Um sumarið segir Gamla-Manga: „Þetta sumar er löng og ljót saga.“ Og Siggi svarar: „En það er engin kviða. Sóttin kann ekki að yrkja.“
words_with_history.note_en: kviða 'narrative poem' belongs with kveða 'to say, chant' (kvað, kvæði): a kviða is something chanted. Many Eddic poem titles end in it: Þrymskviða, Hymiskviða, Völundarkviða.

grammar.note_en: Eddic verse I: reading Þrymskviða. The target is receptive: you recognise and unpack verse; you never write it. Þrymskviða ('the Lay of Þrymur') is an Eddic poem in fornyrðislag, the commonest Eddic metre. 1. Lines and alliteration. Each short line has two stressed syllables, and the lines go in pairs joined by alliteration (stuðlasetning): stressed words that begin with the same sound. The first line of a pair has one or two stuðlar 'props' (síns; Hló, Hlórriða); the first stressed word of the second line is the höfuðstafur 'head-stave' (saknaði; hugur). Any vowel alliterates with any other vowel (æsir / argan; Einn, át / átta), and hl alliterates with h (Hló Hlórriða / hugur). Ásta's joke „Siggi og sjúklingur … sóttin“ plays on this. There is no end rhyme. 2. Free word order. Verse puts words where the metre wants them: a genitive before its noun (síns hamars = hamars síns 'his hammer', brúðar líni 'a bride's linen'), the verb at the end of the line (síns hamars um saknaði), the subject late (Reið varð þá Freyja). To read a line, find the verb, then its subject, then the rest, and say it in prose order (óbundið mál 'unbound language', prose), as Siggi does after each passage. The case endings, not the position, tell you who does what. 3. Expletive um (in editions also of). In old verse, um often stands before a verb or participle and adds nothing to the meaning: um saknaði = saknaði, um fólginn = falinn 'hidden', um heimtir = heimtir 'gets back', um þekkti = þekkti. It fills the metre: leave it out. It is not the preposition um 'about, around' (+ acc.). 4. Negation on the verb. Old poetry can say 'not' with a suffix on the verb. Sáka ég = sá-k-a ég 'I did not see': sá 'saw' + -k (an old short form of ek 'I') + -a 'not'; in prose, Ég sá aldrei / ekki. Only -a occurs in this chapter's passages; the related suffixes -at and -t (for example varat 'was not') work the same way and are left for a later reading (an owner question in OPEN.md). The old pronoun vætr 'nothing' is another negative: Át vætr Freyja = Freyja át ekkert. 5. Other old words in the passages: engi = enginn 'no'; und = undir 'under'; hví = af hverju 'why'; kveld = kvöld 'evening'; heiti for Þór: Vingþór, Hlórriði; kennings for Þór: Sifjar verr 'Sif's husband', Óðins sonur 'Óðinn's son'. The poem is printed here in modern spelling (ég and fyrir, where editions have ek or eg and fyr). The prose paraphrases in the story are the key to every passage, and nothing in these tables is for production. Translations of the tables. Verse → prose: og síns hamars / um saknaði 'and he missed his hammer' → því að hann saknaði hamarsins síns 'because he missed his hammer'; átta röstum / fyrir jörð neðan 'eight leagues below the earth' → Þrymur faldi hamarinn átta röstum undir jörðinni 'Þrymur hid the hammer eight leagues under the earth'; Reið varð þá Freyja / og fnásaði 'then Freyja grew angry and snorted' → Freyja varð svo reið að hún fnásaði 'Freyja grew so angry that she snorted'; Mig munu æsir / argan kalla 'the gods will call me unmanly' → Æsirnir kalla mig argan 'the gods call me unmanly'; leggið Mjölni / í meyjar kné 'lay Mjölnir in the maiden's lap' → leggið Mjölni á kné meyjarinnar 'lay Mjölnir on the maiden's knees'. Alliteration: Einn át uxa, / átta laxa 'one (the bride) ate an ox, eight salmon'; Hló Hlórriða / hugur í brjósti 'Hlórriði's heart laughed in his breast'. um and -a: um saknaði 'missed'; um fólginn 'hidden'; um þekkti 'recognised'; Sáka ég 'I did not see' (ég sá ekki); Át vætr 'ate nothing' (át ekkert).

pronunciation_note.rule: hv at the start of a word is said [kv] in most of Iceland: hvass [kvasː]. kv in kviða and kvef is plain [kv]. ll after a vowel is [tl̥]: stuðull [ˈstʏːðʏtl̥]. öl has a long vowel before a single l: [œːl]. Stress always falls on the first syllable: MISlingar, HÖFuðstafur, ÚTbrot, UTanbókar. In verse the stressed syllables carry the alliteration: SÍNS hamars / um SAKnaði. No audio is supplied.

provenance.author: Claude Opus (story and apparatus, 2026-11-15)
provenance.prompt: Story and apparatus by Claude Opus from the row-36 brief, continuing Kafli 35 (afi died in January 1882; the Edda is now Siggi's; Hallur wintered at Hamrar and taught Siggi verse) and Kafli 16 (the Þrymskviða play: Óli the bride, Ásta Freyja, Siggi Þrymur, Helga Loki, Manga the giant's sister).
provenance.review_required: Independent linguistic and historical review; draft only, no human review claimed.
notes: Source of the embedded reading: Þrymskviða (Codex Regius), quoted in part in modern normalised spelling from the standard text (Netútgáfan and the Íslenzk fornrit / Eddukvæði modern-spelling editions), receptive, each passage followed by Siggi's prose-order paraphrase. Stanzas used (numbering of the common editions; Netútgáfan's numbering differs by one in places, e.g. the „Látum und honum“ passage is its stanza 16): 1 (lines 1–5), 7–8, 13, 15/16 (keys, women's clothes, knees), 17, 20, 24 (lines 1–6 and 9–10), 25, 26, 27, 29, 30 (lines 3–6), 31, 32. Normalisations from Netútgáfan's modern spelling: eg → ég, fyr → fyrir, Mjöllni → Mjölni, Sák-a eg → Sáka ég. About 190 words of verse and 230 words of paraphrase and comment (receptive cap about 400 with paraphrases, design §7.6).

Modernisation forced by the checker: ek/eg → ég and fyr → fyrir (the analyser rejects eg and fyr as non-BÍN forms with an accent suggestion). The owner may prefer the edition's forms; see review questions.

G36 (receptive): alliteration taught in the story (stuðull, höfuðstafur, s040–s042, s096–s097); free word order and expletive um explained by Siggi (s038); the -a negation (Sáka ég, s080–s081); vætr (s084). -at and -t are named only in the grammar note (no example in the chapter's passages): a proposed deferral, put to the owner in OPEN.md, not decided here. Verse items in the workbook and Pensum A are recognition items (mode recognition): verse → prose choice; nothing asks for verse production. The Skrifaðu (x5-2) is closed: a gapped prose version of stanzas 25–26.

Declared incidentals for the verse: vætr and Sáka (BÍN has no entries), so that recognition items can quote the lines; both are explained in the story. Vingþór is added to course.json names (Vingþór, Vingþórs). Other old forms (nam, und, lukla, kvenváðir, bifðist, kveldi, verr, sáld, óðfús, öndótt, arma, harðhugaður, skell, skillinga, endur) are covered by verse glosses only and are never tested.

Learner-load ledger: 49 new lexemes (47 single words, 2 phrases: hlúa að, lifa af) against a budget of 58 (ceiling 63). Planned but not used: þjást (the analyser lemmatises its forms as BÍN þjá, so they never license is-thjast), gneisti, ásynja; open slots uns, átt, blíður, fagna, innan, upphiminn not used (fjöld, hvass, fólginn and aldinn are used). New inflected forms of known lexemes: none beyond G01–G35; the verse adds only receptive old forms. Aids: 38 margin glosses (about 1.85 per 100 words; Hluti 4 window 0.5–2): 21 on verse lines or old forms, 17 on new words; 5 define (13%). New-token share about 8%. Running words about 2,055 (window 1,683–2,057; at the top because of the recall carrier and the paraphrases; never padded).

Recall carrier (row 36): the funeral (útför, in Hofteigur; Siggi read his vísa at afi's grave, s010), the household devotions (húslestur, s009, s026), sál, heiti, kenning, yrkja, sótt, háski (s023) all in the first two sections; Siggi reads verse because afi taught him heiti and Hallur taught him to compose (s010, s040).

History: 1882 was mislingasumarið; the measles came by ship in the spring and spread across the country; those who had had measles in the great epidemic of 1846 were immune (there was also a smaller eastern outbreak in 1869; the family's children are taken to have escaped it, fiction), which is why Manga (born 1799), Bjarni and Guðrún do not fall ill while Siggi and Ásta (born after 1846) do. That measles reached Jökuldalur in summer 1882, the priest's warning, the suspension of services at Hofteigur and several funerals there are plausible but unverified [?]. Sea ice off the north and east and a cold summer with sleet in July are in the history brief (1882 'very cold with very poor grass').

Recycle focus used (row 36): mæta, lýsa, hversu, vísa, krefja, gjald, skot, för, látinn, merkja, hleypa, réttur (Rétt), auka (jókst), hár (háan hita, háan fald), mæla, áhugi, helvíti, blessaður, heiti, kenning, sál, útför, springa, veröld, hrinda, söknuður, kerra, engill, yrkja, guðsþjónusta, taumur, kirkjugarður, vígja; not used: ár 'oar', líking; patterns G05, G13, G27 throughout. Carry-over words not used: líking, grunnur, reyndar, vöðvi, sund, stöng, vængur, hneta, félag, kæra.

Warnings left: media-count (0 inline scenes; text-only release, images not attempted because of HTTP 402), media-coverage for nouns with in-text routes, write-length (at the top of the window), grammar-unlicensed for aðrir and þriðju (both licensed in use: G20 ordinals; annar as pronoun), lexicon-plan first-lesson mismatches in other chapters, recycle-missing (carry-over).

review_questions.quote: Vorið eftir að afi dó kom hafísinn aftur að landinu …
review_questions.question: History [?]: sea ice and sleet in July 1882 at Hamrar; the brief has 1882 as very cold with very poor grass. The exact weather in Jökuldalur that summer is unverified.

review_questions.quote: Með skipunum kom líka sótt til landsins. Það voru mislingar.
review_questions.question: History [?]: measles came to Iceland by ship in spring 1882 and spread across the country in the summer; whether and when it reached Jökuldalur, and the funerals and suspended services at Hofteigur (s008), are plausible fiction.

review_questions.quote: „Mislingarnir komu líka fyrir mörgum árum,“ sagði Manga. „Ég fékk þá, en ég dó ekki.
review_questions.question: History: the great Icelandic measles epidemic before 1882 was 1846 (a smaller eastern outbreak followed in 1869); Manga (born 1799) would have had it at 47; Bjarni and Guðrún (born about 1832) as children. That they are immune and the children are not is the medical point of 1882 [H for 1846; the family's case is fiction].

review_questions.question: Text and staging [?]: stanza 15–16 (Netútgáfan 16; Heimdallur's advice; Kafli 16 had Guðrún play Heimdallur). The keys at the waist as the housewife's sign are the standard reading; Guðrún's explanation (s059) and her mother's faldur at her wedding (s060) are invented. The tall white faldur is the bridal headdress of the old faldbúningur; Siggi now qualifies it (s062): the poem says the gods put something high on his head („ok hagliga um höfuð typpum“), and he takes it to be a faldur.

review_questions.question: Text [?]: stanza 32, lines 1–2 and 5–8; lines 3–4 („hin er brúðféar / of beðit hafði“) are replaced by „…“; the last two lines are s100.

review_questions.quote: „Hló, Hlórriða, hugur, hamar,“ sagði Ásta. „Allt byrjar á sama hljóði.
review_questions.question: Metre: in stanza 31 the alliteration of the first pair is Hló, Hlórriða / hugr and of the second pair harðhugaðr / hamar; Ásta lists the h-words across both pairs, and Siggi names only the first pair (s097). hl alliterates with h.

review_questions.quote: Um morguninn var ennið blautt af svita, og hitinn var farinn.
review_questions.question: Plot (row 36): the fever breaks the night she laughs. A sweat at the crisis of a measles fever is the folk picture; medically the fever falls as the rash fades, which s106 also shows („útbrotið var orðið fölt“).

review_questions.quote: „Helvíti,“ sagði hann lágt. „Enginn þurrkur. Grasið visnar, og ærnar eru magrar. Kindurnar deyja á heiðinni. Ég fann sex dauðar í dag.“
review_questions.question: Hook (payoff Kafli 37): sheep dying on the heath in a cold summer; the number six is invented [?]. Bjarni's curse echoes Manga's line in Kafli 35's Orð með sögu.
